blocks.text: I can understand the stages of the Statistical Enquiry Cycle.

items.title: Evaluating the cycle
items.sub: spot skipped stages and weak plans

blocks.text: Tap the term to see what it means.

items.def: The Statistical Enquiry Cycle is a cycle used to carry out a statistical investigation. There are five stages. This is an ongoing process as evaluation may lead to new/refined questioning.

blocks.text: When a statistical investigation takes place, a model of the process can be used. Imagine you want to find out how often families have a takeaway.

items: Plan the enquiry and ask a question, for example: how often do families have a takeaway?
Collect data to answer the question, for example with a survey or questionnaire, or from a secondary source such as a company that delivers takeaways.
Organise and present the data in a chart or diagram.
Analyse the data: look at the charts for significant findings and complete summary statistics such as the mean, median, mode and range.
Interpret the analysis in the context of the enquiry question.
Use the findings to refine the enquiry question or to take action.

blocks.text: A more formal model of the Statistical Enquiry Cycle has only five stages. Organising, presenting and analysing the data join together into one stage.
It is a {cycle}: evaluation may lead to a new or refined question, and then you go round again.
What does the planning stage involve?

items: Defining a question or hypothesis to investigate.
Deciding what data to collect, and how to collect and record it.
Deciding how the data will be processed and represented.

blocks.text: In the planning stage you think about all of the other stages of the process.
What does the collecting stage involve?

items: Gathering the data. This could be first hand or from other sources.
Considering how data on sensitive subjects may have challenges.

blocks.text: What does the processing and presenting stage involve?

items: Organising and processing the data, which might need to be cleaned, potentially making use of technology.
Generating diagrams and charts to represent the data, potentially making use of technology.

blocks.label: What does “cleaning” data mean?
blocks.text: Spreadsheet software struggles if answers contain unexpected characters. If one person types “6 hours” you remove the word “hours” so only the 6 is left. If another types “30 minutes” you must choose one unit: turn 30 minutes into a half hour, or turn 6 hours into 360 minutes.
What does the interpreting stage involve?

items: Analysing the diagrams, charts and statistical measures in the context of the problem.
Reaching conclusions, making inferences and/or predictions related to the statistical question or hypothesis.
Considering the reliability of the findings.

blocks.text: What does the communicating and evaluating stage involve?

items: Identifying weaknesses in the approach or the representations.
Suggesting improvements to the processes.
Refining the processes to get further information about the initial statistical question or hypothesis.

blocks.text: This is why it is a cycle: you might go through it again to iron out flaws, or to investigate something interesting you found.

slides.title: Match the event to the stage

blocks.q: Match each event to the stage of the Statistical Enquiry Cycle it belongs to.

pairs.a: Deciding the question to investigate and which chart to use
Drawing a bar chart of the results
Looking at the results and deciding what they show
Spotting a weakness in the approach and suggesting improvements

items.q: Which stage comes straight after Collecting?
Which stage comes straight after Interpreting?
Which stage comes first when you begin an enquiry?
Sam has planned his enquiry and gathered his data. What is the next stage?
Considering whether the findings can be trusted (their reliability) belongs to which stage?
Removing the word “hours” from typed answers so a spreadsheet can read them belongs to which stage?
A teacher wants to see whether the hours a pupil revises and their test mark are related. Which chart fits when processing and presenting the data?

blocks.text: Andeep wants to investigate whether 15-year-old pupils are eating fruit and vegetables regularly. He asks ten 15-year-olds from his school two tick-box questions: how many portions of fruit or vegetables they ate yesterday, and on how many days in a week they eat at least one portion.

He flicks through the responses and concludes that 15-year-olds are not eating fruit and vegetables regularly, because most pupils did not eat at least one portion on more than half of the days in a week.

blocks.label: Planning and collecting
blocks.text: His planning was quite limited but had a focus: he knew who he would ask and how. He did not decide how to process or represent the data. He asked ten pupils, a fairly small sample but one he could easily reach.

blocks.q: Which stage of the cycle did Andeep not really complete?
blocks.why: He only flicked through the ten responses. He could have looked at the modal response to each question and drawn a bar chart.

blocks.label: Watch out!
blocks.text: Skipping the processing and presenting stage may lead to false conclusions, or to missing something interesting in the data that could be explored further. All stages should be completed.
Izzy wants to know the favourite colour of the pupils in her school. She asks 5 of her friends and shows the results on a scatter graph. She says: “Purple is the favourite colour!”

blocks.q: Which stage does each comment belong to?

items.q: She should have planned more thoroughly who to ask, how to collect and record the data and how to process it.
A scatter graph was the wrong choice of representation. A pie chart or a bar chart would have been a much better choice.

blocks.text: Laura compares javelin throws by Year 10 and Year 11 pupils (eight throws each). She only calculates the mean and concludes that Year 10 pupils are better.

items: Mean: Year 10 17.925 m, Year 11 17.92375 m. Year 10 is only slightly higher.
Median: Year 10 17.42 m, Year 11 19.76 m. Year 11 is higher.
Range: Year 10 6.31 m, Year 11 15.45 m.

blocks.label: What went wrong?
blocks.text: The mean is affected by extreme values. One very short throw of 5.87 m made the Year 11 mean lower. Laura should have used the median, which is not affected by extreme values.

items: The Statistical Enquiry Cycle has five stages: planning, collecting, processing and presenting, interpreting, and communicating and evaluating.
Planning defines the question and what data to collect. Collecting gathers the data.
Processing and presenting calculates statistical measures and draws charts. Interpreting reaches conclusions.
Communicating and evaluating identifies weaknesses and improvements. All stages should be completed to avoid false conclusions.

flashcards.front: What is the Statistical Enquiry Cycle?
flashcards.back: A cycle used to carry out a statistical investigation. It has five stages.

flashcards.front: Name the five stages of the Statistical Enquiry Cycle in order.
flashcards.back: Planning, Collecting, Processing and presenting, Interpreting, Communicating and evaluating.

flashcards.front: What does the planning stage involve?
flashcards.back: Defining a question to investigate and deciding what data to collect (how to collect and record it, and how it will be processed and represented).

flashcards.front: What does the collecting stage involve?
flashcards.back: Designing collection methods and gathering the data, first hand or from other sources.

flashcards.front: What does the processing and presenting stage involve?
flashcards.back: Calculating statistical measures and making graphical representations (charts and diagrams). The data may need cleaning first.

flashcards.front: What does the interpreting stage involve?
flashcards.back: Reaching conclusions and making inferences or predictions about the question, and considering how reliable the findings are.

flashcards.front: What does the communicating and evaluating stage involve?
Why is it called a cycle?
flashcards.back: Evaluation may lead to a new or refined question, so you can go round again.
Making the data ready for a spreadsheet, for example removing the word “hours” from “6 hours” and using the same unit for every answer.

flashcards.front: Which stage of the cycle decides which charts will be used?
What can happen if you skip the processing and presenting stage?
flashcards.back: You may draw false conclusions, or miss an interesting element of the data.

flashcards.front: Which average is affected by extreme values, and which is not?
flashcards.back: The mean is affected. The median is not.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: The Statistical Enquiry Cycle
worksheet.instructions: Answer each question with a number or a short word or phrase.

questions.prompt: How many stages does the (formal) Statistical Enquiry Cycle have?
questions.explanation: The five stages are planning, collecting, processing and presenting, interpreting, and communicating and evaluating.

questions.prompt: Which stage comes first in the Statistical Enquiry Cycle?
questions.explanation: You start by planning what you want to find out and how.

questions.prompt: The last stage is called “Communicating and …”. Which word is missing?
questions.explanation: The fifth stage is communicating and evaluating.

questions.prompt: Which stage involves gathering the data, either first hand or from other sources?
questions.explanation: Collecting is about gathering the data.

questions.prompt: Which stage involves reaching conclusions and making inferences about the question?
questions.explanation: Interpreting means analysing the results in the context of the problem and reaching conclusions.

questions.prompt: Removing the word “hours” from typed answers so a spreadsheet can read them belongs to which stage?
questions.explanation: Cleaning the data is part of processing the data.

questions.prompt: One person wrote “30 minutes” for time spent watching television. What is 30 minutes as a number of hours (as a decimal)?
questions.explanation: 30 minutes is half of 60 minutes, so 0.5 hours.

questions.prompt: Another person wrote “6 hours”. How many minutes is 6 hours?
Izzy showed the favourite colours of her friends on a scatter graph. Name a type of chart (two words) that would have been a much better choice.
questions.explanation: A pie chart or a bar chart would have been a much better choice, because there were not two sets of data that might be related.

questions.prompt: Which is not affected by extreme values, the mean or the median?
questions.explanation: The mean is affected by extreme values but the median is not.
